situational5.title: Situational writing · eight more tasks with models
situational5.instruction: Read the situation twice before you write. Underline the three bullet points — those are the marks. Decide formal or informal before your first word, then write 60 to 120 words. Write your own answer first; only then uncover the model and the note underneath it.

bands.label: 8–9 · All four points covered, each with a supporting detail
6–7 · All four covered, but one or two are thin
4–5 · Three points covered
2–3 · Two points covered
0–1 · One point, or largely off task
6 · Correct format, consistent tone, almost no errors
5 · Correct format, a few errors, tone mostly right
3–4 · Format mostly right, several errors or tone slips
2 · Format or tone clearly wrong, frequent errors
0–1 · Hard to follow

tasks.task:
You left your water bottle in the school hall after assembly yesterday. Write an email to Mr Siva, who looks after the lost property cupboard.

You should include:
• what you lost and where
• how he will know it is yours
• when you can collect it

Write about 70 to 90 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to claim a lost item. Audience: a teacher you do not know well — formal, but not stiff. Context: he has a cupboard full of bottles, so the describing bullet is the one that earns the marks.
tasks.model:
Dear Mr Siva,

I am writing about a water bottle I left in the school hall after assembly on Tuesday morning. I think it was under the third row of chairs, near the side door.

It is a dark blue metal bottle with a dented lid, and my name, Rayyan Osman, is written in marker on the base. There is also a badminton sticker on one side.

May I collect it during recess on Thursday? I have PE after recess, so I would be grateful to have it back by then.

Thank you.

Yours sincerely,
Rayyan Osman
tasks.why: Every bullet is answered with something only the owner would know: the row of chairs, the dent, the name on the base, the sticker. The collecting bullet adds a reason, which is what turns a request into a polite one. Formal opening and closing are matched — 'Dear Mr Siva' with 'Yours sincerely'.

tasks.task:
Your mother has gone out and you have to leave for football training before she returns. Write her a note.

You should include:
• where you have gone and when you will be back
• what you have already done at home
• one thing you need her to do

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to leave instructions. Audience: your mother — warm and informal. Context: she will read it in a hurry, so short lines and clear times.
tasks.model:
Mum,

I have gone to football training at the field behind the community centre. It ends at 6.30 p.m. and I should be home by seven.

I have hung out the washing and fed Biscuit. His bowl is washed and back under the sink.

Could you sign my reading record before tomorrow? It is on the dining table, next to my pencil case. Mrs Chia collects it first thing in the morning.

Love,
Isaac
tasks.why: Informal does not mean vague. Two exact times answer the first bullet, two completed jobs answer the second, and the request names the document, where it is, and why it cannot wait. No greeting formula is needed for a family note, but it still opens and signs off.

tasks.task:
You bought a school bag two weeks ago and the zip has broken. Write an email to the shop.

You should include:
• what you bought and when
• what has gone wrong
• what you would like the shop to do

Write about 80 to 100 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to have something put right. Audience: a shop you have no relationship with — formal and unemotional. Context: they need enough facts to find the sale, so dates and names matter more than feelings.
tasks.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I bought a navy Haversack Junior school bag from your Tampines branch on 28 September. The receipt number is 4471.

The main zip has come away from the fabric on the left side, so the bag can no longer be closed. It has been used only for school, and nothing heavier than books has been carried in it.

As the bag is only two weeks old, I would like it exchanged for the same model. If that is not possible, a refund would be acceptable.

I can bring the bag and the receipt in on any Saturday.

Yours faithfully,
Priya Raman
tasks.why: The complaint works because it is calm. The facts needed to trace the sale come first, then exactly what failed and where, then a preferred outcome with a fallback. 'Dear Sir or Madam' is closed with 'Yours faithfully' — the pairing to use when you do not know the name.

tasks.task:
You have been invited to your friend Wei Ming's house to work on a group project. His father asked you to email him the details. Write the email.

You should include:
• when you and the others will arrive
• what the project needs
• one question about the arrangements

Write about 70 to 90 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to confirm arrangements. Audience: a friend's father — polite but not as formal as a letter to a stranger. Context: he is the one planning around you, so your details must be definite.
tasks.model:
Dear Mr Lee,

Thank you for letting us work at your home on Saturday. Three of us will come — Dinesh, Clara and I — and we will arrive at two o'clock and leave by half past four.

Our project is a model of a water treatment plant, so we will bring cardboard, glue and two plastic bottles. We will need a table and, if possible, a plug for the glue gun.

May I ask whether we should remove our shoes at the door?

Thank you.

Yours sincerely,
Clara Ng
tasks.why: Semi-formal means full sentences and a proper sign-off, but the content can be friendly. All three bullets carry a number or a name: three people, two exact times, the materials listed, one clear question. Asking about shoes shows awareness of the host, which is the kind of detail that lifts tone marks.

tasks.task:
Your class would like to keep a small vegetable garden in the empty plot behind the canteen. Write a letter to your principal.

You should include:
• what you are asking for
• why it would be good for the school
• who would look after it

Write about 90 to 110 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to persuade someone who can say yes or no. Audience: the principal — the most formal audience in the paper. Context: she will worry about cost and about who does the work when you move up a year, so answer both without being asked.
tasks.model:
Dear Mrs Rahman,

I am writing on behalf of Primary 5 Resilience to ask whether we may use the empty plot behind the canteen as a small vegetable garden.

We would grow kangkong, chilli and basil. The canteen could use what we harvest, and our Science topic next term is plant growth, so we would be studying outside instead of from a worksheet.

Six of us have volunteered to water the beds in pairs before school. Our form teacher, Mr Siva, has agreed to supervise, and we will hand the garden on to the next Primary 5 class in January.

Thank you for considering our request.

Yours sincerely,
Nadia Zainal
(on behalf of Primary 5 Resilience)
tasks.why: A request to a principal needs to answer the objection before it is raised. The benefit is specific (the canteen, the Science topic), the labour is organised (six pupils, in pairs, before school), and the long-term worry is settled in one clause about January. Writing 'on behalf of' makes clear this is not one pupil's idea.

tasks.kind: Email · to a librarian (formal, P4 level)
tasks.task:
You cannot return a library book on time because you are away. Write an email to the school librarian, Miss Goh.

You should include:
• which book you have
• why you cannot return it
• when you will bring it back

Write about 60 to 70 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to explain and ask. Audience: a teacher — formal. Context: three short bullets, one detail each. Keep the sentences simple and correct rather than long.
tasks.model:
Dear Miss Goh,

I borrowed The Sea Beneath Us on 1 October. It is due back this Friday.

My family is away in Penang for my grandmother's birthday and we return on Sunday evening, so I cannot bring the book in on Friday.

May I return it on Monday morning before assembly? I am sorry for the delay, and the book is safely in my bag.

Thank you.

Yours sincerely,
Mei Qi
tasks.why: At Primary 4 the marks come from covering the points cleanly, not from long sentences. The title and the borrowing date identify the book, the reason is given with a return date that makes it believable, and the new date is offered as a question rather than an announcement.

tasks.task:
You are the chairperson of the Green Club. Write a notice inviting pupils to a used-book sale.

You should include:
• when and where the sale will be held
• what pupils should bring or do
• what the money will be used for

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to inform a crowd quickly. Audience: every pupil in school. Context: a notice is read standing up, so the heading and the details must do the work. No 'Dear' and no 'Yours sincerely' — but it must say who wrote it.
tasks.model:
USED-BOOK SALE

The Green Club is holding a used-book sale on Friday, 24 October, from 1.00 p.m. to 3.00 p.m. in the hall foyer.

Every book costs one dollar. Bring coins, as we cannot give change for notes. If you have books to donate, leave them in the blue box outside the staff room by Wednesday.

All the money raised will buy saplings for the garden behind Block B.

Green Club Committee
tasks.why: A notice is judged on how fast a reader can find the facts, so the day, the times and the place come in the first sentence. The practical warning about change is the sort of detail a real notice carries. It ends with the body responsible, which replaces a signature.

tasks.task:
Your cousin in Johor is deciding whether to join you at a holiday camp in Singapore. Write an email to persuade her.

You should include:
• what happens at the camp
• why she would enjoy it
• what she would need to arrange

Write about 80 to 100 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to persuade someone who is undecided. Audience: a cousin your own age — informal, warm, contractions allowed. Context: persuading works better with one vivid detail than with three adjectives.
tasks.model:
Hi Suhana,

You have to come to the camp! It runs from the 3rd to the 6th of December at Changi, and each day has two activities — kayaking in the morning and a cooking or craft session after lunch. On the last night everyone sleeps in tents on the field.

You kept saying you wanted to try kayaking, and the instructors take complete beginners. Mei Qi is coming too, so you would already know two of us.

You would need to ask your parents about the ferry and bring a sleeping bag. Let me know by Sunday so I can book you a place.

See you soon!
Farah
tasks.why: The persuading is done by facts, not by the word 'fun': exact dates, named activities, the tents on the last night. The middle bullet reaches for something the reader has already said she wanted — the strongest persuasive move available. The deadline at the end gives her a reason to reply.

composition3.title: Continuous writing · six more model compositions
composition3.instruction: Write the whole composition yourself first — six minutes to plan, forty to write, no notes. Then read the model and the note underneath it and mark yourself on both scales: 20 for content, 20 for language. Two of the tasks carry a shorter Primary 5 model as well, so you can see the same story told in about 170 words.

bands.label: 17–20 · Fully relevant, a clear and interesting plot, well-developed characters and feelings
13–16 · Relevant with a clear plot; some development of feelings
9–12 · Mostly relevant; the plot is thin or rushed in places
5–8 · Partly relevant; events listed rather than told
0–4 · Largely irrelevant to the theme or the pictures
17–20 · Varied sentences, accurate tenses, precise vocabulary, almost no errors
13–16 · Generally accurate; some variety; a few errors that do not obscure meaning
9–12 · Simple sentences, repeated structures, several errors
5–8 · Frequent errors; meaning sometimes unclear
0–4 · Meaning often lost

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about a time when you kept trying after failing.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a bicycle lying on its side • a maths worksheet covered in red marks • a pair of hands holding a skipping rope.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: the failure in paragraph one, the lowest point in two, the decision to try again in three, the attempt in four, the result and what changed in five. Put the feeling in the body, not in the last line.
tasks.model:
The first time I tried, I lasted four seconds. I know it was four because my brother counted them out loud.

The bicycle was too tall for me. My father had bought it second-hand from a neighbour, and its frame was the dull red of a rusting gate. Every time I pushed off, the handlebars twisted and the ground came up to meet my elbow.

By the ninth try I had stopped wanting to ride it. I sat on the kerb with grit in my palms and told my father I was finished with bicycles for good. He did not argue. He simply lowered the seat by two centimetres and went inside.

It was the two centimetres that annoyed me. If the bicycle could be changed, then so, it seemed, could I.

I tried again the next evening, and the evening after that. On the Thursday I wobbled the whole length of the carpark and stopped by putting both feet down hard, which is not how it is done, but it counted.

I still cannot turn tightly. I can, however, get to the end of the carpark, which four seconds of me would not have believed.
tasks.p5model:
The first time I tried to ride the bicycle, I fell after four seconds. My brother counted.

The bicycle was second-hand and too tall for me. Every time I pushed off, the handlebars twisted and I landed on my elbow. After nine tries I sat on the kerb and told my father I was finished with bicycles.

He did not argue with me. He only lowered the seat a little and went inside. That annoyed me. If the bicycle could be changed, perhaps I could change too.

I tried again the next evening, and the evening after that. On Thursday I rode the whole length of the carpark. I stopped by putting both feet down hard, which is not the proper way, but I did not fall.

I still cannot turn corners well. But I can reach the end of the carpark now, and that is more than I could do on the first day.
tasks.why: The marker is looking for a plot, not a lesson. The ending reports what changed rather than announcing a moral, and the feeling is carried by concrete things — the counted seconds, the grit in the palms, the two centimetres. The father is developed in two actions and no dialogue, which is enough. Tense is consistently past; the one present-tense sentence at the end is deliberate, because it is still true now.

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about a time when a stranger helped you or someone you know.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a bus stop in heavy rain • a dropped bag of groceries • an old man with a walking stick at a kerb.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: set the scene and the problem in one, make the problem worse in two, bring in the stranger in three, the help itself in four, and in five the small thing you still remember. Do not let the stranger give a speech.
tasks.model:
The rain started as we left the market, and by the time we reached the bus stop it was coming down so hard that the road had turned to a grey sheet.

My grandmother does not walk quickly. She was carrying one bag and I was carrying two, and the handle of the heavier one had already begun to stretch. At the shelter we discovered that the bus we needed had been diverted, and that the nearest stop was now two hundred metres further on.

Then the bag gave up. It split along the bottom and emptied itself — onions, a packet of noodles, four oranges rolling out into the rain like something escaping.

A woman in a yellow raincoat was waiting with us. She did not say anything heroic. She crouched down, began gathering the oranges into the front of her own shopping bag, and said, 'Hold this corner.'

Together we carried everything to the new stop under her umbrella, which was far too small for three people.

I never learnt her name. What I remember is that she asked me to hold the corner — as though I were helping her, and not the other way round.
tasks.why: The kindness lands because the stranger is understated: one instruction, no speech, no thanks demanded. Paragraph three is the climax and is given its own short paragraph, which is how pace is controlled. The final line interprets a small detail instead of stating that kindness matters. Notice the comparison 'like something escaping' — one image is plenty.

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about a time when you had to choose between two things that both mattered.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: two tickets on a table • a mobile phone showing a message • an empty seat in a classroom.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: name the two choices in one, show why each matters in two and three, the moment of deciding in four, the cost of it in five. A decision story needs the loss shown, or there was no decision.
tasks.model:
The two tickets lay on the table all week, and I looked at them every time I passed.

My uncle had bought them for the Saturday match, the one we had talked about since August. He had already told the neighbours. He had already explained to me, twice, where our seats were in relation to the goal.

On Wednesday, Clara's mother told my mother that Clara's competition had been moved to Saturday afternoon. Clara had been practising her piece since the March holidays. She had asked me, not quite asking, whether I would be there.

I did not decide for two days. I made lists in my head, and the lists kept coming out even, which is the worst answer a list can give.

On Friday night I told my uncle. He was quiet for a second and then said the match would be on television, which was kind and not quite true, because he had wanted to go together.

I sat through Clara's piece in a cold hall on a plastic chair. She played well and she saw me. I thought about the match twice.

It was the right choice. It was still a choice that cost something, and I think that is what made it one.
tasks.p5model:
The two tickets lay on the table all week. My uncle had bought them for the Saturday match, and we had talked about going since August.

Then on Wednesday I found out that Clara's piano competition had been moved to Saturday afternoon. She had been practising since the March holidays, and she had almost asked me to come.

I could not decide for two days. Whenever I listed the reasons, both sides came out the same, which was no help at all.

On Friday night I told my uncle I would go to the competition. He was quiet for a moment and then said the match would be on television. I knew he had wanted us to go together.

I sat on a plastic chair in a cold hall and listened to Clara play. She played well, and she saw me in the audience.

It was the right choice, but it still cost me something. Perhaps that is what makes something a real decision.
tasks.why: Both options are given real weight — the uncle has told the neighbours, Clara has practised since March — so the decision is genuinely hard. 'The lists kept coming out even' shows thinking without describing it. The uncle's line is reported with the narrator's reading of it, which is how a character is developed cheaply. The ending admits a cost instead of tidying it away.

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about something you found that you were not looking for.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: an old tin box • a photograph in a library book • a key with no label.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: ordinary task in one, the find in two, what it looked like in three, what it turned out to mean in four, and what you did with it in five. The discovery should change how you see a person, not produce treasure.
tasks.model:
We were clearing the storeroom because the ceiling had begun to leak, and everything in it had to come out onto the corridor floor.

The tin box was at the bottom of a crate of cables. It was the size of a shoebox, pale green, with a picture of a biscuit factory on the lid and a dent in one corner.

It was not locked. Inside there were no coins and nothing valuable: twenty or thirty paper tickets, each one a bus ticket, each one with a date written on the back in pencil.

My mother looked at them for a long time before she explained. My grandfather had come to the city alone at sixteen and had taken the same bus to the same factory for nine years. He had kept one ticket from each payday, she said, because that was the day he sent money home.

I had known my grandfather as a slow man in a brown armchair who fell asleep during the news. I had not known there had been nine years of that bus.

The box is in our cupboard now, above the plates. We did not throw out a single ticket.
tasks.why: The find is worthless in money and valuable in meaning, which is the better choice for this theme. The description is three details, not a catalogue: size, colour, dent. Paragraph five does the real work — it contrasts the grandfather the narrator knew with the one the tickets reveal, and that contrast is the story. The last sentence is short and factual, and carries the feeling because of it.

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about a time when you were put in charge of something.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a younger child holding your hand • a classroom key • a fish tank.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: the job you were given in one, what you thought of it in two, the moment it went wrong in three and four, what you did in five. Responsibility stories are only interesting when something is nearly lost.
tasks.model:
Mrs Chia gave me the key on a Monday, in front of everybody, and said only, 'Last one out, lights off.'

For two weeks it was the best thing about school. The key lived in the small pocket of my bag and I checked for it at every change of lesson, pressing the outside of the pocket with my thumb.

On the Thursday of the third week I went to badminton straight after the last bell. I remembered the room at a quarter past five, in the middle of a rally, and the remembering was like stepping into cold water.

I ran back with my racket still in my hand. The lights were on, the windows were open, and Suresh's new reading glasses were sitting on his desk, where anybody could have taken them. Nobody had. That was luck, and I knew it was luck.

I closed the windows, turned off the lights and locked the door. Then I did the part I did not want to do, which was to tell Mrs Chia the next morning before she asked.

She let me keep the key. I think the telling was the reason.
tasks.why: The near-miss is kept small and real — open windows and a pair of glasses, not a theft. 'The remembering was like stepping into cold water' puts the feeling in an image. The hardest part of the story is given its own sentence: owning up before being asked. The ending does not explain the moral; 'I think the telling was the reason' lets the reader finish it.

tasks.prompt:
Write a composition about a time when you were frightened.

Your composition must be based on ONE of these three pictures: a dark corridor • a sudden thunderstorm at a beach • a lift that has stopped between floors.

About 150–200 words for Primary 5, 200–250 for Primary 6.
tasks.plan: Plan: ordinary start in one, the first sign of trouble in two, fear building in three, the worst point in four, the rescue in five, and one line after. Describe what your body did instead of saying you were afraid.
tasks.model:
The lift had stopped between the fourth and the fifth floor, and the number on the panel was showing neither.

I pressed the button for the fifth again, the way you do, as though the lift had simply forgotten. Nothing happened. The fan above me, which I had never once noticed in eleven years of living in that block, stopped as well, and the silence it left behind was the first thing that frightened me.

I counted the panels on the ceiling. There were six. I counted them three times. My hands were cold and the back of my neck was not, and I could hear my own breathing, which is a strange thing to be able to hear.

I pressed the orange alarm. It rang somewhere far away, in a room I have never seen, and then a man's voice asked me which block I was in. I could not remember the number of my own block. He waited while I worked it out.

The technician came in eleven minutes. He opened the doors with a tool like a bicycle spanner and I stepped up onto the fifth-floor landing.

I still take the lift. I just look at the ceiling panels when I do, and there are always six.
tasks.why: Fear is shown almost entirely through the body and through small useless actions — pressing the button again, counting the panels three times, forgetting the block number. The stopping of the fan is a better scare than any adjective. The rescue is deliberately unheroic, with a named tool and an exact number of minutes. The last line returns to the panels, which ties the piece together without a moral.
